defects.why: يتداخل هذا المقطع مع درس المسار الآخر «قبل النوبة: الجوع والنعاس والانتقال المفاجئ» الذي يغطي الجوع والنعاس والانتقال المفاجئ قبل النوبة، فيضعف تميّز الدرس.
تغفل هذه القائمة علامة الخطر «يصعب تهدئته» الواردة في وحدة المعرفة؛ فقد يحتاج الطفل الذي يصعب تهدئته إلى تقييم طبي حتى لو لم يؤذِ نفسه أو لم تكن النوبات شديدة ومتكررة.
صياغة إنجليزية متكلفة؛ الترجمة الأدق لعبارة «هدوء سريع» هي quick calm.

lessons.brief: قبل النوبة: الجوع والنعاس والانتقال المفاجئ
lessons.title: قبل النوبة: الجوع والنعاس والانتقال المفاجئ

defects.why: استخدام «عليه» بعد «شعور قوي» غير دقيق وقد يوحي بأن الشعور ضدّه؛ الأصوب «لديه» أو «يغمره».
«لتنتهي النوبة» قد تُفهم خطأً أن الغاية أن تنتهي النوبة وليس أن تغيير القرار هو الوسيلة؛ الأوضح «لإنهاء النوبة».
«صرف انتباهك عنه» تركيب ملتبس؛ قد يُقرأ «صرف انتباهه عنك» والأوضح «أمّا تجاهلك إيّاه».

lessons.brief: بعد أن يهدأ: الحضن أولًا ثم الكلمات

defects.why: الضمير «ها» يعود على «لمسة» المؤنثة فقط، فيُفهم أن الشرط خاص باللمسة دون الحضن، والصواب أن يشمل الاثنين.
الدرس مخصص لما بعد نوبة الغضب الكاملة، لكن try_this يقول «أول لحظة غضبٍ أو بكاءٍ» وهو أوسع نطاقًا وقد يطبّق على انفعال بسيط لا يستدعي كل هذه الخطوات، ما يخلّ بدقة الربط بين الملخص والفعل المطلوب.

lessons.title: بعد أن يهدأ: الحضن أولًا ثم الكلمات

defects.why: The Arabic says «ولا أنك أخطأت في تربيته» — 'made a mistake/erred in raising him' — which is gentler than 'failed in raising them'. 'Failed' overstates the Arabic and adds a tone of finality not present in the original.
«أيّ» صيغة مذكّرة، والصواب مع «القصّتين» المؤنثة «أيّة القصّتين».
صياغة متكلّفة بعض الشيء؛ الأوضح «كثير المطالب وصعب الإرضاء».

safety_changes: s03: safety first; hitting, biting, kicking, throwing or self-harm stopped at once, calmly and without violence, never ignored (AAP/CDC/AACAP); hold a child rushing into danger (AAP)
s03: check tiredness, hunger, pain or starting illness and meet the need first (AACAP/NHS/CDC)
s03: stay close, give time and space, few calm words; no shouting, hitting, threats or humiliation (CDC/AACAP/NHS/AAP)
s03: gentle hug only if more sad than angry and the parent is calm (NHS)
s03: do not give in or bribe with sweets after a reasoned no (NHS/CDC)

s03: turning attention away only from minor, safe attention-seeking behaviour such as whining, while watching, attention returned as soon as it stops; never for hunger, tiredness, illness, pain, fear or distress (CDC)
s03: parent's own pause with the child in a safe place or with a trusted adult (AAP/CDC)

s03/s04: talk with the pediatrician if very frequent or longer than expected for age, cannot calm down, harm to self (on purpose) or others/danger, disrupts daily life, lost skills (AACAP/CDC milestones); s04 adds persistently sad, withdrawn, or very demanding and unsatisfied most of the time (AAP); urgent help for serious injury or when safety cannot be kept (seed-tantrum-23)

s04: both calm first; closeness before words (hug if wanted, gentle touch, eye contact, smile); name the feeling, accept correction; validate feeling, limit behaviour, two simple choices; do not rush to solutions (CDC emotion coaching/AAP/NHS)
s04: if they hit: 'hitting hurts, I will not allow it'; never hit back (NHS); no shaming or reproach, return to warmth and praise words (AAP/CDC/NHS)

primary_sources.used_for: AAP (served as 'Top Tips for Surviving Tantrums'): tantrums normal; do not ignore hitting, kicking, biting, throwing; stop it immediately; hold a child in danger; distraction; give yourself a break; talk with your pediatrician
AAP: spanking, yelling and shaming harmful; parent's own time-out with the child in a safe place, then hug and start over; never take away something the child truly needs
AAP: anger erupts as tantrum, may hit, bite or kick; consult pediatrician if very withdrawn, perpetually sad, or highly demanding and unsatisfied most of the time

AACAP: tired, hungry, pain, mild illness; remain calm (modeling); words not unsafe actions; distraction; state calmly which behaviour must stop; never physically aggressive; seek help for danger, self-harm, not calming, very frequent/longer than expected, interfering with life (minute figures not used)
CDC: ignoring only for minor safe attention-seeking behaviour (whining); never needs-based, distress or danger; do not leave alone unless safe; return attention when it stops

CDC: ensure safety, remain close, hands free, time and space; wait until both calm; notice, connect (eye contact, smile, touch), name the emotion, accept correction; validate feelings and limit behaviour; do not rush to solutions; parent's pause or another trusted caregiver
CDC: giving in rewards the tantrum; spanking, yelling and embarrassing are unhealthy; go back to being positive
CDC: teach acceptable ways to show they are upset; praise positive behaviour
CDC: lost skills or other concerns -> talk with the child's doctor

NHS: find out why (tired, hungry); shouting back will not end it; do not change your mind or bribe with sweets; distraction; holding when more upset than angry and you are calm; do not hit back, make clear hitting hurts; 'I know you're feeling angry'; praise and cuddles; GP if seriously concerned

removed_from_original_drafts: s05: 'whoever completely crushes stubbornness ... postpones the confrontation to later years' (not in fetched sources)
s05: 'a rule applied once and dropped once teaches resisting works' replaced by CDC/NHS consistency and follow-through wording

s05: 'gentleness (rifq) is strength not weakness' and 'a child whose will is respected in small things learns to respect limits in big ones' (rhetoric not in sources; no religious content in these lessons)
s05: limits named as 'safety, sleep and cleanliness' -> safety and harm to others (AAP: draw the line at dangerous or antisocial behaviour)
s06: 'one of the most effective tools', 'their refusals drop a lot', 'you will notice the small daily battles easing ... your voice calmer' (promised outcomes) -> choices may help, no guarantee
s06: 'stubbornness at this age usually comes from the need to feel in control' -> AAP 'give your child control over little things'
s06: 'many options confuse a small child' (not in sources) -> small, simple choices (AAP/CDC)
safety_changes: s05: repeated 'no' framed as showing independence and testing limits (CDC 'terrible twos'/early years; AAP), not a verdict on child or parent; the parent's feeling of rejection named as normal (CDC)
s05/s06: check tiredness, hunger, pain or starting illness, frustration or boredom first and meet the need (NHS/AACAP)
s05: few clear limits held consistently for safety and harm to others, explained simply ('hold my hand when we cross the street', NHS); flexible on small harmless matters (AAP choose your battles)
s05: a calm statement instead of a yes/no question when 'no' is not an option (AAP); make a resisted routine more fun such as a bath toy (CDC)
s05: same response every time, same approach among caregivers, follow-through (CDC/NHS); specific praise (CDC/AAP/NHS); no reward before the behaviour (NHS: a bribe)

s05: no hitting, shouting, threats or humiliation; hitting teaches that hitting is acceptable (NHS/AAP); parent's pause taken close to the child or with a trusted adult staying with the child (CDC/AAP; reviewer medium fixed)

s06: two choices both acceptable to the parent instead of a yes/no question or a bare order (AAP; CDC 'carrots or an apple'); no choice where safety is concerned, e.g. the car seat every ride (CDC), with a choice offered elsewhere
s06: tell the child beforehand what will happen (CDC predictability; AAP prepare them)
s06: if they choose neither: needs first, then the parent decides calmly and follows through without long negotiation, shouting or threats; no sweets to make them choose (CDC follow-through; NHS)
s06: choices may help but do not prevent every refusal or tantrum; return to safety and calm

s05/s06: talk with the pediatrician if very frequent or longer than expected for age, cannot calm down, harm to self or others, disrupts daily life, lost skills, withdrawn, sad, or very demanding and unsatisfied most of the time (AACAP/CDC milestones/AAP); urgent help for serious injury or when safety cannot be kept (seed-tantrum-23); no minute, month or count thresholds

primary_sources.used_for: CDC: 'terrible twos' as toddlers begin to assert their independence; car seat with a harness; teach acceptable ways to show upset
CDC: developing emotional and physical independence can look like pushing away; parents may feel frustrated or rejected, this is normal; pause; adjust expectations
CDC: consistency, predictability, follow-through ('do what you say you will do'); make a resisted routine more fun (bath toy or bubbles); explain changes calmly
CDC: specific (labeled) praise
CDC: simple choices, 'Do you want carrots or an apple?'
CDC: lost skills -> talk with the child's doctor
CDC: a pause, or another trusted caregiver for a longer pause
AAP: control over little things with small directed choices rather than yes/no questions; choose your battles; consistency; specific praise

AAP: two-year-olds test limits; consistently set reasonable limits, draw the line at dangerous or antisocial behaviour; praise when they dress themselves; consult the pediatrician if very passive or withdrawn, persistently sad, or highly demanding and unsatisfied most of the time

AAP: clear consistent limits in age-appropriate terms; toddlers test rules; prepare children for upcoming activities; choices among acceptable alternatives; no spanking, yelling or shaming; parent's own time-out with the child safe
AAP: describe and praise real effort; do not ignore unsafe behaviour (touch counts and minute figures not used)

NHS: tired, hungry, frustrated or bored; consistency, everyone close to the child the same way; explain why (hold hands crossing the road); specific praise; a reward before is a bribe; smacking teaches hitting is OK
NHS: do not change your mind or bribe with sweets; shouting back will not end it
AACAP: tired, hungry, pain, mild illness; remain calm; seek help for danger, self-harm, not calming, very frequent or longer than expected, interfering with life (minute figures not used)
